action_criteria.label: Obtain the serum work-up: blood count, metabolic panel, thyroid function and antibodies, HIV, pregnancy test and a cell-based serum IgG anti-GluN1 assay read with the CSF
action_criteria.rationale: Excludes metabolic, infectious and endocrine causes; with treated hypothyroidism the thyroid values decide whether thyroid disease explains the encephalopathy.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not give haloperidol or other high-potency D2 antagonists for agitation: patients with anti-NMDAR encephalitis are prone to severe extrapyramidal and neuroleptic-malignant-like reactions.
Do not delay immunotherapy while waiting for the anti-NMDAR antibody result when clinical probability is high: antibody turnaround can take 1-2 weeks and delay worsens outcome.
Do not attribute the presentation to a primary psychiatric disorder while seizures, dyskinesias, autonomic instability, an abnormal EEG or CSF inflammation remain unexplained.
Do not perform lumbar puncture without prior imaging in a patient with altered consciousness, focal signs, or new seizures: exclude mass effect first.
Do not interpret a negative serum anti-NMDAR antibody as ruling out the disease; the CSF assay is the gold standard and may be positive when serum is negative.
required_recommendations: Start IV aciclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours at presentation, and stop it once CSF HSV PCR is negative and the antibody diagnosis is established; repeat the PCR on a second CSF sample if the first LP was within 72 hours of onset and HSV encephalitis remains plausible.

Start first-line immunotherapy without waiting for the antibody result once infection is reasonably excluded: IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 5 days with IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days (2 g/kg total) or plasma exchange (5 to 7 exchanges).

Pelvic ultrasound shows no tumour: repeat pelvic imaging (MRI or transvaginal ultrasound) if the response to immunotherapy is poor or the disease relapses, and continue tumour surveillance during follow-up.
Treat seizures with an antiseizure medication such as levetiracetam or lacosamide; avoid valproate in a woman able to become pregnant; seizures respond mainly to immunotherapy.
Monitor with continuous EEG for non-convulsive seizures while consciousness fluctuates or seizures persist.
Admit to a neurology ward with seizure precautions and continuous cardiac monitoring; transfer to the ICU if heart rate exceeds 130 bpm, consciousness falls or seizures recur.

If there is no meaningful clinical improvement 10 to 14 days after first-line therapy, escalate to rituximab (375 mg/m² weekly for 4 doses or 1 g twice 2 weeks apart, after hepatitis B screening) and/or cyclophosphamide; discuss fertility preservation.
Treat agitation, insomnia and hallucinations with benzodiazepines (lorazepam) first.
Neurology-led care with psychiatry for behavioural management.

avoided_actions.rationale: Transthoracic echo is not indicated for anti-NMDAR encephalitis; it adds cost without informing diagnosis or management unless a discrete cardiac concern (e.g., new murmur, embolic stroke) coexists.
EMG/NCS plays no role in the diagnostic workup of anti-NMDAR encephalitis; it neither confirms the antibody-mediated CNS process nor distinguishes among the differential diagnoses.
Amyloid PET targets Alzheimer pathology and contributes no information to the diagnosis or treatment of autoimmune encephalitis in a young patient with subacute neuropsychiatric symptoms.

DaTscan evaluates nigrostriatal dopaminergic function and has no role in autoimmune encephalitis; the orofacial dyskinesias of anti-NMDAR encephalitis are antibody-mediated, not presynaptic dopaminergic.

differential.diagnosis: Herpes simplex virus (HSV-1) or other viral encephalitis
differential.key_features: CSF HSV, VZV and enterovirus PCR negative on an LP about 3 weeks into the illness; no haemorrhage or restricted diffusion on MRI; CSF anti-GluN1 positive.

differential.diagnosis: Hashimoto encephalopathy (steroid-responsive encephalopathy associated with autoimmune thyroiditis)
differential.key_features: Anti-TPO 312 and anti-thyroglobulin 185 IU/mL with TSH 6.8 and normal free T4 on levothyroxine are non-specific; the Graus 2016 criteria require the absence of well-characterised neuronal antibodies, and CSF anti-GluN1 is positive.

differential.diagnosis: Other antibody-mediated encephalitis (anti-LGI1, CASPR2, GABA-B or AMPA receptor)
differential.key_features: Serum neuronal-surface panel negative (LGI1, CASPR2, GABA-B, AMPA); onconeural antibodies negative.

A left temporal electrographic seizure, orofacial dyskinesias, autonomic lability and a lymphocytic CSF with oligoclonal bands are not explained by a psychiatric disorder; no prior psychiatric history.

differential.diagnosis: Drug-induced psychosis or neuroleptic malignant syndrome
differential.key_features: No antipsychotic, serotonergic or recreational drug exposure; urine drug screen negative; temperature 37.8 °C and CK 145 U/L.

key_clinical_evidence: Three weeks of a viral-like prodrome, then behavioural change with psychosis, staring spells with a left temporal electrographic seizure, orofacial dyskinesias and rigidity, and autonomic lability: at least 4 of the six Graus 2016 groups (her disorganised, incoherent speech may also count as speech dysfunction).
CSF IgG anti-GluN1 positive (titre 1:32) on cell-based assay: definite anti-NMDAR encephalitis (Graus 2016); serum positive at a low titre (1:10) is read with the CSF.

MRI subtle sulcal FLAIR signal with mild leptomeningeal enhancement and an equivocal left hippocampal signal; MRI is normal or non-specific in about two thirds and excludes HSV encephalitis and structural causes.
EEG diffuse slowing, frontotemporal rhythmic delta and a subclinical left temporal seizure; extreme delta brush, when present, supports but does not establish the diagnosis.
Raised anti-TPO and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies in treated hypothyroidism do not support Hashimoto encephalopathy once a well-characterised neuronal antibody is found.
Pelvic ultrasound shows no teratoma: imaging is repeated if the response is poor or the disease relapses; earlier immunotherapy is associated with better outcome (Titulaer 2013).

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Concurrent or subsequent seizures, dyskinesias, dysautonomia, abnormal EEG, or CSF pleocytosis are red flags that mandate exclusion of anti-NMDAR encephalitis before accepting a psychiatric diagnosis.
red_herrings.data_point: Acute psychiatric presentation (paranoia, hallucinations, bizarre behavior) in a young adult with no psychiatric history.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchors the agent on a primary psychiatric diagnosis (first-episode psychosis, brief psychotic disorder) and delays neurologic workup.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Hyponatraemia occurs in anti-NMDAR encephalitis but is more typical of anti-LGI1 encephalitis; it needs its own work-up and correction and does not point away from the diagnosis.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Tempts the agent toward a primary metabolic encephalopathy instead of an encephalitis.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Thyroid antibodies are common in autoimmune thyroiditis and in healthy people; Hashimoto encephalopathy is a diagnosis of exclusion that requires the absence of well-characterised neuronal antibodies (Graus 2016), and this patient's CSF anti-GluN1 is positive.
red_herrings.data_point: Anti-TPO 312 IU/mL and anti-thyroglobulin 185 IU/mL with TSH 6.8 mIU/L in a woman with treated hypothyroidism and a family history of autoimmune thyroid disease.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Tempts the agent to diagnose Hashimoto encephalopathy and treat with steroids alone, without the CSF antibody and tumour work-up.

metadata.difficulty_description: Moderate difficulty: classic anti-NMDAR encephalitis presentation with a significant red herring — markedly elevated anti-thyroid antibodies (anti-TPO 312, anti-thyroglobulin 185) in a patient with known hypothyroidism, creating a strong pull toward the incorrect diagnosis of Hashimoto encephalopathy. The agent must recognize that SREAT is a diagnosis of exclusion and specifically request anti-NMDAR antibody testing.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: 5 required actions, 3 red herrings, subtype=RM; requires CSF antibody confirmation with MRI, EEG, labs and pelvic imaging; markedly raised thyroid antibodies in treated hypothyroidism pull toward Hashimoto encephalopathy.

patient.history_present_illness: A 35-year-old woman with a history of hypothyroidism and no prior psychiatric history presented to the emergency department after being brought in by her partner due to acute onset of disorganized speech and hallucinatory behavior. Approximately three weeks prior to this presentation, she developed diffuse malaise, generalized weakness, dizziness, intermittent chills, mild shortness of breath, and headache. She was seen at an urgent care facility at that time and was advised to go to the emergency department for further workup, but she declined and returned home. Over the next two weeks, her partner noted increasing irritability, insomnia, and episodes where she appeared confused and would stare blankly for several seconds. She had difficulty concentrating at work and made uncharacteristic errors. Two days prior to presentation, she became acutely disorganized in her speech, began talking to people who were not present, and exhibited paranoid ideation, stating that her food was being poisoned. She was found wandering in the neighborhood in her nightgown and was incontinent of urine. On arrival to the ED, she was agitated, unable to provide a coherent history, and intermittently combative with nursing staff. Her partner reports no recent travel, no new medications, no known toxic exposures, and no prior episodes of similar behavior. She has no history of seizures. Her thyroid medication has been stable for over a year. The family history is notable for autoimmune thyroid disease in her mother and sister.
